_readme: The same two-entry pattern with authorization on. TWO INDEPENDENT MECHANISMS are at play and confusing them is the usual mistake:

1. CLIENT authorization (OAuth 2.1, MCP_BROKER_AUTH_ENABLED). Protects the client HTTP surface: /<slot>/mcp, /<slot>/sse, /<slot>/messages. Entry 2 is on that surface, so it needs a token. Entry 1 is NOT: it speaks over the pipe the host already owns, so it is authorized by the fact that the host spawned it. The broker does not ask a stdio bridge for a bearer token, and there is nowhere to put one.

2. PROVIDER authentication (MCP_BROKER_PROVIDER_SECRET). Protects the two WebSocket provider endpoints, so a stranger cannot occupy a slot. Independent of item 1: turning one on does not turn the other on. It is checked from the X-Provider-Token or Authorization header of the WebSocket upgrade request.

A BROWSER-HOSTED PROVIDER CANNOT USE MECHANISM 2 AT ALL. The browser WebSocket constructor cannot set request headers, and the broker accepts the secret only from a header. Setting MCP_BROKER_PROVIDER_SECRET locks every browser page out of every slot. Use it when all your providers are server-side; put browser providers behind network isolation or client OAuth instead.

The Authorization header on entry 2 below is a STATIC token, which is what most hosts can express. A real deployment normally uses the host's own OAuth flow against MCP_BROKER_PUBLIC_BASE_URL instead; the broker publishes the protected-resource metadata that flow needs at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource.

auth.enabled additionally requires publicBaseUrl, jwks, and at least one authorization server (or issuer). Missing any of them, the broker exits 1 at startup and says which. See .mcp-broker/config.auth.json next to this file.
